newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania inaugurates free trade zone on Danube.
newsitem.headline: Romania inaugurates free trade zone on Danube.

text.p: Romania has officially launched a free trade zone on the Danube River in a bid to boost trade and attract foreign investors to an area near the big markets of Ukraine and Russia, an official said on Monday.
"Starting today, this area has a status of a free trade zone," Radu Driscu, head of the state-owned Zona Libera Galati (ZLG) said during the inauguration ceremony.
Under a government project to turn the area into a major free trade zone, the ZLG was allotted in 1994 in a total of 137 hectares (338 acres) to be developed in coming years.

Last year, the ZLG auctioned some 15 hectares of this area. The winning bidders so far had built warehouses and a line to assemble containers for sea transport, ZLC sources said. Plans to build two oil terminals in the free trade area were also being considered, they said.
A shortage of funds has so far delayed plans by the zone's administration to complete the infrastructure on 30 hectares earmarked for the first stage of the project, ZLC sources said.

The ZLG is located in the new port of the steel town of Galati, 250 km (156 miles) north-east of Bucharest, on the River Danube and has berths allowing ships of up to 50,000 deadweight tonnes to perform operations under a free trade area status.
"I'm confident Western traders will be attracted by the ZLG to use this area as a spingboard for their business with both Romania and the ex-Soviet republics," Driscu said.

The ZLG, located near the border crossings with Ukraine and the former Soviet republic of Moldova, also has rail tracks which can accommodate railway carriages used by all ex-Soviet republics, he said.
The Galati area also has significant economic potential including shipbuilding, machine building, food processing and farming as well as Romania's biggest steel plant.

A 1993 law allows local and foreign investors to lease land and buildings within Romania's free trade zones for periods of up to 50 years. Businesses in the free trade areas are exempt from profit and value added taxes as well as customs and excise duties for the same period.
